cards.text: The Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has been looking hard at life under the sun. Now he tells a little story he calls great wisdom. There was a small city with only a few men in it.

cards.question: Trouble is coming for that small city with only a few men. Who comes against it?

cards.text: A mighty king surrounds the city and builds large siege ramps against it. Friend, that's like showing up to a cookie bake-off with one spatula while the other guy rolls in with a WHOLE FACTORY.

cards.question: The small city is surrounded and the siege ramps are going up. Who saves the city?
After the poor wise man saves the city by his wisdom, everyone remembers him.

cards.text: Nobody remembered that poor man. He saves the WHOLE CITY and doesn't even get a thank-you note, and after my years in the back of a junk drawer, believe me, friend, I know that kind of forgotten.

cards.question: The Teacher says wisdom is better than strength. But what happens to the poor man's wisdom?

answers.text: People despise it and ignore his words
Kings write it down to use later
The city pays him gold to hear it

cards.text: Then the Teacher compares two voices: the calm words of the wise, and the shouts of a ruler among fools. One sounds like a quiet bakery at dawn. The other sounds like my oven timer going off at full blast.

cards.question: The Teacher says the shouts of a ruler among fools are heeded over the calm words of the wise.

cards.text: Next the Teacher says wisdom is better than weapons of war. Then he adds a warning.

cards.question: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one ___ destroys much good.

cards.text: Now a picture. Somebody's fancy perfumer's oil gets a few dead flies in it, and the whole thing stinks. EXPENSIVE stink, friend.

cards.question: What is the Teacher's point with the dead flies in the perfumer's oil?

answers.text: A little folly outweighs wisdom and honor
Perfume should always be kept covered
Wise men should stay far from flies

cards.text: A wise man's heart inclines to the right, but a fool's heart inclines to the left. Then the fool heads out for a walk down the road.

cards.question: As the fool walks along the road, he manages to keep his folly hidden from everyone.

cards.text: Now some advice for a tense day at work: the ruler's temper flares against you. The boss is FIRED UP, his face is the color of my oven light, and everybody in the room is eyeing the door.

cards.question: When the ruler's temper flares against you, do not abandon your ___, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.

cards.text: Then the Teacher names an error that comes from the ruler: folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions. Mr. Reply-All just got promoted to CEO.

cards.question: The Teacher describes a world flipped upside down. What has he seen?

answers.text: Slaves on horseback and princes on foot
Priests in fields and farmers in temples
Soldiers at feasts and kings at the gate

cards.text: Now every job comes with a risk: he who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake. And I thought MY biggest work hazard was a hot oven.

cards.question: The Teacher says the one who splits logs is perfectly safe.

cards.text: If the axe is dull, you have to put more strength into every swing. Baker, I KNOW dull: my edges got so soft that Mother Miller had to press TWICE as hard just to get one blurry cookie.

cards.question: A dull axe takes more strength. So what does the Teacher say produces success?
A snake charmer still profits if the snake bites before it is charmed.

cards.text: Now the Teacher talks about talking. The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious.

cards.question: A wise man's words are gracious, but the lips of a fool ___ him.
The Teacher follows a fool's talk from beginning to end. How does it go?

answers.text: Starts foolish and ends even worse
Starts foolish and ends up wise
Starts wise and ends up foolish

cards.text: Yet the fool multiplies words. He's the guy who sends forty-seven texts to the group chat to say ONE thing, and then a voice memo to explain the texts.

cards.question: Right after the fool multiplies words, the Teacher says no one knows what is coming.

cards.text: Then the fool goes to work, and his toil just wears him OUT.

cards.question: Why does the fool's toil wear him out?

answers.text: He does not know the way to the city
He carries heavy stones for the king
He works all night without any rest

cards.text: Then the Teacher turns to whole lands. Woe to the land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning.

cards.question: Blessed is the land whose king is a son of nobles and whose princes feast at the proper time. What do those princes feast for?

answers.text: For strength and not for drunkenness
For praise and not for peace
For show and not for hunger

cards.text: Now the Teacher looks at a house. One roof caves in, and another house leaks.

cards.question: Through ___ the roof caves in, and in the hands of the ___ the house leaks.

cards.text: That's the drip in the ceiling you promised to fix next weekend, three years ago. Then the Teacher says a feast is prepared for laughter and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything.
Last word from the Teacher: do not curse the king, even in your thoughts. And do not curse the rich, even in your bedroom.

cards.question: The Teacher says not to curse the king or the rich, even in private. Why not?

answers.text: A bird of the air may carry your words
The palace walls hear every word
The king can read every heart

cards.text: A little bird carrying your words straight to the king. Friend, that's the ORIGINAL group chat leak, and it didn't even need a phone.

findings.problem: This story card only repeats Ecclesiastes 9:15, which cards 4 and 5 already covered, and adds a joke. It doesn't move the passage forward. It also tells the baker the poor man got no thanks at all, which rules out the wrong answer 'The city pays him gold to hear it' on card 7 before the baker reaches it.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: The setup on card 6 ('doesn't even get a thank-you note') rules out the wrong answer 'The city pays him gold to hear it', which makes the question too easy.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences ('Then the Teacher compares…', 'One sounds like…', 'The other sounds like…').

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Verse 9:17 is about which voice gets heeded. The comparison only contrasts quiet with loud, and an oven timer at full blast is something people do pay attention to. The picture works against the verse's point, and that could mislead the baker on the true/false question in card 9.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The story card before this one gives nothing to reason from. In a verse about weapons of war, 'soldier' fits the blank as well as 'sinner', so the baker is guessing the wording of the line rather than reasoning out its meaning.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences ('Now a picture.', 'Somebody's fancy perfumer's oil…', 'EXPENSIVE stink, friend.').

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card drops the verse's 'If' and states as a fact that 'the ruler's temper flares against you.' It also frames verse 10:4 as 'advice for a tense day at work' and swaps the ruler for 'the boss' in the same breath. That blends the modern comparison into the Bible setting.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: The question changes the BSB's 'If the ruler's temper flares against you' to 'When the ruler's temper flares against you.' Card 16 also leaves out the 'if'.
'Now every job comes with a risk' turns the Teacher's specific examples (pit digging, breaching a wall, quarrying, splitting logs) into a general claim about every job. Verses 10:8-9 never say that.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Card 1 has just said 'every job comes with a risk,' which gives away the answer to 'the one who splits logs is perfectly safe' (False).

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The joke changes the backstory. papa-dorin.md says Mother Miller 'just pressed a little harder,' but the card says she 'had to press TWICE as hard.'

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The question asks whether a particular line comes 'right after' the fool multiplies words. The baker can't reason that out from earlier cards, so it is a guess about the next line's wording. The second half of 10:14 ('who can tell him what will come after him?') is also never told.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: 'One roof caves in, and another house leaks' says there are two different houses. Verse 10:18 is a parallel saying ('the roof… the house'), and the text never says they are separate houses.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This last story card only repeats 10:20, which card 19 already covered, and adds a joke. It works as a recap card and doesn't tell any new part of the passage.
